site.name: Positive
site.intro: Five small retellings from India’s living story traditions. Read one, then return to your day a little lighter.

stories.title: The Four Friends of the Island
stories.source: More Jataka Tales (Ellen C. Babbitt, 1922) — Project Gutenberg #7518, Story XIII
body: On a small island in the middle of a quiet lake, a family of Hawks made their home high in a shady tree, and on the three shores lived their dear friends—a Lion, a Kingfisher, and a gentle Turtle. Every evening the father Hawk flew out to greet them, and the four companions shared the warmth of the lake together.

One night, hunters camped beneath the Hawks' tree and plotted to eat the young birds at dawn. The Kingfisher flew swiftly among them, beating out every fire with his wings until he could beat no more. Then the Turtle dove deep, gathered cool mud, and smothered the next flame; when the hunters tried to net him, he pulled them tumbling into the deep water after him.

At last the Mother Hawk called for the Lion, whose mighty roar shook the island and drove the hunters far away. The young birds were safe. The Kingfisher and Turtle came ashore to join the Hawks at the foot of the tree, and the four friends praised one another softly as the morning light returned.

stories.title: Four Visits, One Tree
stories.source: More Jataka Tales (Ellen C. Babbitt, 1922) — Project Gutenberg #7518, Story IX
body: Four young princes set out one after another to be the first to see the famous Red-Bud Tree near their father's palace. The eldest found only a bare, dark trunk in early spring, so dark it looked like a ghost of a tree. He hurried home sure no such beauty could exist.

When the second prince arrived, the branches blazed with red buds like tiny flames. The third brother came later to find soft green leaves rustling in the wind, while the youngest, walking there in late summer, found the tree heavy with ripe bean-pods, plump and ready to be gathered.

Back at the palace the brothers quarreled, each certain the others were mistaken about what they had seen. The king listened quietly, then smiled and told them they had all visited the same beloved Red-Bud Tree in four different seasons. His gentle wisdom hushed their arguing and taught them a hopeful truth.

stories.title: The Clever Old Goat's Triumph
stories.source: More Jataka Tales (Ellen C. Babbitt, 1922) — Project Gutenberg #7518, Story XVIII
body: High on a sun-baked hillside, two hungry Wolves had picked off every Goat in the cave save one wise old fellow who always slipped their snares. At last they tried a clever ruse: the male Wolf stretched out stiff and still as though dead, while his mate came bleating to the Goat, begging her help to bury him. The wise old Goat listened, wary but willing, agreeing only on one condition.

She told the Wolf she would come, but the Wolf must walk ahead of her down the path. When the hidden Wolf lifted his head to see if she was following, she caught his glinting eye and fled safely back to the cave. Undeterred, the pair tried once more, creeping closer to her shelter.

Then the wise old Goat called out the names of her imaginary companions, Old Gray and Young Tan, and the great dog Four-Eyes, each with his faithful mate. At the sound of that fierce company, the Wolf turned tail and vanished into the hills. From that day on, the clever Goat lived in peace, her quiet wit the guardian of the last of the herd.

stories.title: The Ox and the Hundred Wagons
stories.source: Jataka Tales (Ellen C. Babbitt, 1912) — Project Gutenberg #62514, Story V
body: A proud owner bragged of his great Ox and wagered a thousand pieces of silver that the beast could pull a hundred wagons in a line. But when the day of the test arrived, the man grew fearful and began whipping his Ox, shouting cruel names at the gentle creature who had only ever known kind words. The Ox stood still and would not move, and the wager was lost.

That night, the Ox spoke gently and asked why his master had changed. Hearing this, the man felt deep shame and begged forgiveness, promising never again to raise his hand or voice in anger. The next morning he fed the Ox sweet fodder, hung fragrant flowers about his neck, and patted him softly along the way.

With kind words and gentle hands, the great Ox pulled all hundred wagons in one smooth, unbroken line. The watching crowd paid back the thousand pieces of silver with joy, and the man and his Ox walked home together, their friendship restored and the Ox's noble worth finally honored by all.

stories.title: Beauty's Careful Herd Returns Whole
stories.source: More Jataka Tales (Ellen C. Babbitt, 1922) — Project Gutenberg #7518, Story XX
body: An old father Deer gathered his two sons, Beauty and Brownie, beneath the wide Indian sky, warning that the ripening rice fields would soon be laced with hidden traps. He urged them to travel only under moonlight, far from any village fire, and to trust the cool darkness for safety.

Beauty listened closely and led his herd only by night, steering them well away from the huts where hunters kept watch. Brownie, forgetting his father's words, wandered through the bright daytime hours past the fields and villages, and one by one his Deer were taken.

When harvest came and the herds returned to the green forest, Beauty's family arrived complete, every gentle Deer accounted for, while Brownie's line was sadly thinned. The father's wisdom shone true, and hope remained with those who walked with care.
